title: Elevator System
summary: Design the controller for a bank of elevators that serves hall and car requests with a pluggable scheduling policy.
description:
An office tower has **N elevators** serving **M floors**. People press an **up/down hall button** on a floor, or a **floor button inside the car**. A central controller decides which elevator serves each hall request.

The building owner wants to experiment with scheduling algorithms (nearest car, least busy, zoning for peak hours) and needs a *maintenance mode* that takes a car out of service.

Focus on the **object model and state**: which object owns which state, how requests flow from buttons to cars, and where the scheduling decision lives.

functionalRequirements.text: Passengers can call an elevator from any floor using Up or Down hall buttons.
Inside a car, passengers can select one or more destination floors.
A central dispatcher assigns each hall request to one elevator using a scheduling policy.
Each elevator tracks its current floor, direction (up/down/idle) and door state.
An elevator can be put into maintenance mode and receives no new requests while in it.
Displays inside cars and on floors show the current floor and direction of each car.

nonFunctionalRequirements.text: The scheduling algorithm must be swappable at runtime (e.g. peak-hour zoning).
Doors must never open while the car is moving.

constraints: Ignore physical motor control — assume a moveTo(floor) primitive exists.
Weight limits and emergency alarms are out of scope.

variationPoints.name: Scheduling policy
variationPoints.description: The rule for choosing which car serves a hall request.

variationPoints.name: Elevator state
variationPoints.description: Behaviour differs when idle, moving, doors-open or in maintenance.

extensionScenario.prompt: The owner adds a VIP express elevator that skips floors 2–20 and a fire mode where every car returns to the ground floor. How does your design absorb these?

hints.title: Who owns what state?
hints.text: Each Elevator owns its current floor, direction and door state. The Dispatcher owns nothing but the decision of which elevator gets a hall call. Keep those apart.

hints.title: Make scheduling pluggable
hints.text: Introduce a SchedulingStrategy interface with something like selectElevator(request, elevators). NearestCar, LeastBusy and Zoned become implementations; the Dispatcher holds a reference it can swap.

hints.title: Model states explicitly
hints.text: Idle, MovingUp, MovingDown, DoorsOpen and Maintenance behave differently. An ElevatorState interface (State pattern) makes illegal actions — opening doors while moving — impossible by construction.
